questions.stem: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in which Part of the Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Constitution is the 'Fundamental Rights' section — enforceable against the State. Part II (Arts 5-11) is Citizenship. Part IV (Arts 36-51) is DPSP (non-justiciable). Part IV-A (Art 51-A) is Fundamental Duties (added by 42nd Amendment, 1976).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) was described by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar as:

options.option_text: 'The heart and soul of the Constitution'

questions.explanation: Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' because without it, the Fundamental Rights would be unenforceable. Article 32 grants citizens the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of FRs via writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto). Article 32 itself IS a Fundamental Right. 'The conscience of the Constitution' is sometimes used for the DPSP+FR combination; 'crown' is used loosely for the Preamble.

questions.stem: Which Fundamental Right was removed from the list by the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978)?
questions.explanation: The Right to Property (originally Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978) during the Janata Party government. It was relocated as a LEGAL right under Article 300-A (Part XII). This reduced the number of FRs from 7 to 6. The other FRs have never been removed, though their scope has been modified.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'Right to Education' was added as a Fundamental Right (Article 21-A) by which Constitutional Amendment?
questions.explanation: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21-A guaranteeing the right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years. Implementing legislation: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009 — came into force on 1 April 2010. 73rd=Panchayati Raj; 93rd=OBC reservation in educational institutions; 101st=GST.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the six Fundamental Rights in the current Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: Six FRs today: (1) Right to Equality (Arts. 14-18); (2) Right to Freedom (Arts. 19-22); (3) Right against Exploitation (Arts. 23-24); (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Arts. 25-28); (5) Cultural & Educational Rights (Arts. 29-30); (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Arts. 32-35). Right to Property was DEMOTED to a legal right (Art. 300-A) by the 44th Amendment (1978) — so it is NOT a Fundamental Right anymore.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees:

options.option_text: Right to life and personal liberty
Equality before law AND equal protection of laws

questions.explanation: Article 14: 'The State shall not deny to any person equality BEFORE the law or the equal PROTECTION of the laws within the territory of India.' Note two distinct guarantees: (1) 'equality before law' — British/Dicey concept, negative — no one is above the law; (2) 'equal protection of the laws' — American concept, positive — equal treatment under equal circumstances. Article 21 is life/liberty. Article 19(1)(a) is speech. Article 21-A is education.

questions.stem: The Right to Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?

options.option_text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)

questions.explanation: The 9-judge bench in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (August 2017) unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21, and is protected under Part III of the Constitution. This case was a reference from the Aadhaar challenges. Kesavananda (1973) = basic structure doctrine. Maneka Gandhi (1978) = expanded Article 21 ('procedure established by law' → must be just, fair, reasonable). Navtej Johar (2018) = decriminalised consensual same-sex relations (Sec 377).

questions.stem: The writ of 'Habeas Corpus' is used to:

options.option_text: Direct a lower court to produce records of a case
Challenge the legality of a person's detention and demand their production before court
Prevent a public servant from exercising an office they have no right to
Direct a public authority to perform its statutory duty

questions.explanation: HABEAS CORPUS (Latin: 'let you have the body') — the court directs the detaining authority to PRODUCE the detained person and justify the detention. If the detention is illegal, the person is released. Used primarily against illegal police detention, preventive detention, etc. Other writs: CERTIORARI = challenge lower court/tribunal order; QUO WARRANTO = challenge authority to hold office; MANDAMUS = command to public authority; PROHIBITION = prevent lower court from exceeding jurisdiction.

questions.stem: Article 17 of the Constitution deals with:
questions.explanation: Article 17: 'Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.' Its enforcement was operationalised through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Article 18 abolishes titles (hereditary honours); Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour; Article 24 prohibits child labour under 14 in factories, mines, and hazardous employment.

questions.stem: During a National Emergency (Article 352), which of the following Fundamental Rights CANNOT be suspended?
questions.explanation: Article 359 (as amended by 44th Amendment, 1978) specifies that during Emergency, the enforcement of FRs (except Articles 20 and 21) may be suspended by Presidential order. Art 20 = protection against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, self-incrimination. Art 21 = life and personal liberty. After the ADM Jabalpur (1976) fiasco — where the SC held Art 21 COULD be suspended — the 44th Amendment explicitly immunised Arts 20 and 21. Today these two rights are NEVER suspendable. Protection in respect of conviction; Life & Liberty.
